skyNotes.saturn: Ringed in ice, bound to give it back.
skyNotes.blackhole: Light turns back; time stands still.

skyStories.saturn:
It wears a ring of ice, and is slowly losing it.
Enceladus breathes a mist of ice from its south pole, laying down a new ring; the old ice falls back into Saturn, grain by grain.
The ring you see is fading and being born at the same time.
skyStories.neptune:
It was found on paper first.
In 1846, someone worked out from the wandering path of Uranus that another world was hiding in the dark. The telescope followed the math, and there it was, as if it had been waiting a long time.
In 1989, Voyager 2 turned on its gravity and never looked back. That bent course, and four arcs of ring that never close, are what it leaves for those who travel far.
skyStories.blackhole:
This is the forbidden zone of the universe.
Light turns back here. Time stops here.
Everything falls in, and nothing finds its way home.
Not one law we have written survives here.
skyStories.betelgeuse:
The shoulder of Orion takes one breath every four hundred days.
With each breath it casts itself into space; the dimming of 2019 was its own dust, veiling its own light.
It is still here, breathing slowly. But one day it will burn out and outshine every night.

light.d: It starts as a sphere and a sun shining from the upper left. The lit side is bright, the far side is dark.

strokes.d: No fill: just rows of horizontal lines, thicker where it is brighter. On the dark side the lines thin out to nothing, leaving only black and white.

bands.d: Brightness follows the bands Cassini photographed: the equatorial zone is brightest, the belts beside it darkest, and the line at 78°N is the edge of the north polar hexagon. A little noise makes the lines waver and break into brush strokes.

rings.d: The rings are concentric strokes too, spaced like the real ones: the B ring is densest, the Cassini Division is empty, and the A ring has the Encke Gap. The planet casts its shadow on the rings, and the rings cast theirs on the planet.

satellites.d: Five orbits outside, one satellite each, matching the five sections on the home page. {{signal}} goes to only one at a time: try tapping another.

trails.d: Last comes the background: with the shutter held open, every star drags an arc around the pole. The notes page keeps this idea, where each post is one star trail.

light.d: It starts as a sphere and a sun shining from the upper left. The lit side is bright, the far side is dark.

strokes.d: Rows of horizontal lines again, but thinner and denser than Saturn's, and almost unbroken: Neptune is wrapped in haze and looks like a smooth ball.

clouds.d: In 1989 Voyager 2 photographed the Great Dark Spot at 22° south, with a white cloud along its southern edge; in 2018 Hubble saw another one in the north. A dark spot is an oval where the lines thin out, ringed by bright cloud. The long bright streaks are high cirrus.

rings.d: The rings are faint, so only the two clearest are drawn: Le Verrier and Adams. The Adams ring has four brighter arcs, named Courage, Liberté, Égalité and Fraternité. Together they span only about 40°; here they are stretched so you can see them.

satellites.d: Five orbits outside, one moon each, matching the five sections on the home page. The fourth is Triton, the only large moon in the solar system that orbits backwards. The fifth is Nereid, with the most eccentric orbit of any moon; it is drawn less stretched here. {{signal}} goes to only one at a time: try tapping another.

trails.d: Last comes the background: with the shutter held open, every star drags an arc around the pole. The notes page keeps this idea, where each post is one star trail.

shadow.d: The black hole itself is invisible. What you see is what it blocks: a shadow larger than the event horizon. The thin photon ring at its edge is light that was pulled around the hole before escaping.

disk.d: Before falling in, matter swirls into a disk. The closer in, the faster, hotter and brighter it is, and the difference in speed drags it into spiral streaks. The disk stops at the innermost stable orbit; anything further in simply falls.

doppler.d: The disk spins at nearly the speed of light: the side turning toward us brightens, the side turning away dims. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope image of M87* is brighter on one side too.

lens.d: The far side of the disk should be hidden behind the shadow, but gravity bends its light around, leaving an image of the disk above and below the shadow. This is how Gargantua looks in Interstellar.

satellites.d: Around the black hole at the center of the Milky Way is a group of stars on tilted, elongated ellipses, and the ellipses themselves slowly turn. Two teams tracked them for thirty years and used them to prove there is a black hole of four million solar masses there, winning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics. The five here match the five sections on the home page. {{signal}} goes to only one at a time: try tapping another.

trails.d: Last comes the background: with the shutter held open, every star drags an arc around the pole. The notes page keeps this idea, where each post is one star trail.

light.d: Betelgeuse is a star: its light comes from itself, so there is no terminator. It is bright in the middle and darker toward the edge, where you are looking at higher, cooler gas.

strokes.d: A planet is engraved row by row along its latitudes, so the lines curve with the cloud bands. A star uses straight horizontal lines across the picture instead, the way an engraving builds up the shading of a sphere.

cells.d: The surface has only a few huge convection cells, bright patches and dark ones; Betelgeuse is one of the few stars whose surface has been imaged directly. The dark patch in the south is the Great Dimming of 2019: it threw off a cloud of material that cooled into dust and blocked its own light.

breath.d: It is a semiregular variable star that swells and shrinks about every 400 days, compressed here into a few seconds. The faint concentric lines around it are its far-reaching atmosphere.

satellites.d: The small dot hugging it is its companion, Siwarha, confirmed only in 2025. Betelgeuse has no known planets; the five dotted lines are the five sections of the home page, drawn as shells of dust it has thrown off. {{signal}} goes to only one at a time: try tapping another.

trails.d: Last comes the background: with the shutter held open, every star drags an arc around the pole. The notes page keeps this idea, where each post is one star trail.

raw.d: One photo from the gallery. A picture taken in space never appears in front of you directly; it has to make the trip down first.

bits.d: The camera turns the image into 0s and 1s and sends them row by row. At first, all you see is this flickering field of digits.

gray.d: The ground station decodes one row at a time. Brightness arrives first, so the photo surfaces from top to bottom. The {{signalLower}} line is the row being received.

color.d: Once the brightness is in, a single sweep from left to right maps the color back. Every photo on the photos page is received this way when it scrolls into view.

dots.d: The same photo with one dot per cell, sized by brightness. Make the cells bigger and the photo slowly turns into a field of stars.

numbers.d: On GitHub, a repo is just a few numbers: how much code, which languages, how many stars and commits, how long since the last push. Try adjusting them.

surface.d: More code makes a bigger planet. The main language picks the surface: TypeScript gives gas bands, Rust cratered rock, Python ice, anything else meridians. More commits mean more bands and craters.

rings.d: Each language beyond the main one adds a ring, with a line style per language: solid for TypeScript, dashed for Rust, dotted for Python. GitHub stars become moons, up to four.

body.d: The works page normally shows only the line symbol; hover and it unfolds into a dotted 3D star, dense on the lit side and sparse on the dark side. The more recent the last push, the faster it spins.

spiral.d: Finally it joins the spiral on the works page: the center is the start, and newer works sit farther out. The one you just made is the newest, so it goes on the outermost turn.
